pairs.evidence: src/features/agents/sub_settings/components/__tests__/SettingsStatusBar.chrome.test.ts:12 This source-text pin regexes the whole SettingsStatusBar.tsx file, comments included, for `<button` and palette class names. Those are needles prose can spell, so a JSX comment explaining the choice would turn it red. The component is also executable in jsdom (SettingsStatusBar.doubleDelete.test.tsx already renders it), so a structural pin was not needed at all.

techniques.evidence: src/features/agents/sub_settings/components/__tests__/SettingsStatusBar.chrome.test.ts:12 Prose can spell the needle and the haystack still contains the file's JSX comments; the technique says 'Where the site can be executed, execute it'. By contrast, assertionConfig.test.ts:17 strips comments before matching.
src/features/agents/sub_settings/components/__tests__/PersonaAssertionsSection.staleList.test.tsx:58 The stale-response race is set up by resolving deferreds in a chosen order, not by timing.
src/features/agents/sub_settings/components/__tests__/PersonaAssertionsSection.staleList.test.tsx:71 The two responses carry different labels, so the assertion shows which producer won.

src/features/agents/sub_settings/components/__tests__/assertionConfig.test.ts:17 The reader is the product's own Rust engine, not a foreign interpreter, so the technique's own exclusion applies. The test reads the struct declaration after stripping comments rather than running serde.
